newsitem.title: USA: Ancient plant source of modern wealth, controversy.
newsitem.headline: Ancient plant source of modern wealth, controversy.

text.p: A New World plant, tobacco was smoked by Mayans at least as long ago as the time of Christ.

And while its popularity spread through Europe and Asia after the Americas and Europe found one another in 1492, only in the 1800s did tobacco in the form of cigarettes became a mass-market consumer product and the stuff from which some of the world's mightiest corporations were created.
"About 20 years later the illnesses we all know about started to appear," said Edward Sweda, an anti-tobacco activist with the Tobacco Control Resource Center in Boston.
Crew with Christoper Columbus, within days of landing after months at sea, began sharing the loosely rolled cigars of the Arawak people of the Caribbean and then took tobacco seeds home to Europe.

Tobacco's two great champions in Europe over the next century were Britain's Walter Raleigh, said to have convinced Queen Elizabeth I to try a smoke, and the French diplomat Philipe Nicot. Nicot's writings from the court of Portugal helped popularize tobacco as a laxative, styptic and a purported cure for gonorrhea.
Tobacco spread to India, the Middle East and China, where it was "smoke blossom". Turkey began growing its own tobacco.
But before governments learned to tax tobacco, many fought its use, with Christian kings denouncing it as an Islamic curse and Moslem rulers saying it was a Christian corruption.

Russia's czar exiled tobacco users to Siberia. Turkey's Sultan Murad IV beheaded smokers after having had a pipe driven through each's nose, and King James I of England taxed tobacco delivered by Spanish galleons at 4,000 percent.

Soon, the British were encouraging their colony Virginia in North America to supply a substitute for Spanish tobacco. Virginian John Rolfe, remembered more for marrying the Powhatan princess Pochantas, acquired tobacco seeds from Trinidad and launched a U.S. industry now four centuries old.

Tobacco so dominated Virginia's economy in the 18th century that wages were paid in tobacco and wives purchased for the going rate of 120 pounds of cured leaf. By the American Revolution in the 1770s, three quarters of the economies of Virginia and Maryland revolved around tobacco.
Some historians said slavery developed largely in the southern United States on plantations created for tobacco.
French for little cigar, the cigarette was first made from the sweepings in Spanish cigar factories and came into its own during the Crimean War and America's Civil War in the mid-1800s.

Few soldiers bought pre-made cigarettes, and neither did many other smokers for decades. One of the few cigarette retailers of the time was Philip Morris, a London tobacconist who died in 1873 but whose name lives on.

With the fitful introduction of a hulking, one-ton cigarette-making machine in the 1880s, the manufacture of tens of thousands of cigarettes a day became practical and allowed -- along with price slashing led by James Buchanan Duke of Durham, North Carolina -- the creation of a mass market for branded, ready made cigarettes.

Machine-rolled, packaged cigarettes arrived on U.S. store shelves as a boom in regionally and nationally distributed consumer products transformed the American economy in the late 1800s. Cigarettes were among the first branded products.

Duke dominated his industry for decades, buying 250 rivals until his American Tobacco Co was broken up by U.S. trust busters early in the 20th century. Duke went on to fund a major university and the Duke Power Co, a leading utility still in the U.S.

Cigarette consumption was most popular in U.S. cities, with New York accounting for 25 percent of American sales in the early 20th century, but cigarette smoking grew steadily. Massive numbers of veterans of World War I and II returned home smokers.

Substantial scientific evidence against cigarette smoking began appearing in the 1950s but did little to hurt sales and consumption. The U.S. government ordered health warnings placed on cigarette packages in 1965 and four years later banned television advertising for cigarettes.

Smoking grew ever more controversial through the 1970s, 1980s, and 1990s, with local governments banning indoor smoking and filing lawsuits against tobacco companies. Individual lawsuits by sick smokers and non-smokers claiming injuries from secondhand smoke mushroomed. More than 1,000 lawsuits now exist against U.S. tobacco companies.

But the business of tobacco thrived, helping Philip Morris become one of the greatest producers of branded consumer goods such as Marlboro. Other leading companies with a big tobacco business are Loews Corp, which until recently controlled the CBS television network, and RJR Nabisco Holdings.
Tobacco's role in the economies of North Carolina, Virginia, Kentucky and many other southern U.S. states remains critical.

"Last year, tobacco accounted for about $2.5 billion in farm receipts in the 17 or 18 states in the U.S. where its grown, and this year receipts should reach about $3 billion," said Professor Will Snell of the University of Kentucky.
Tobacco is the sixth or seventh most valuable crop grown in the United States and an increasingly important export.
"Tobacco accounts for a $5 billion to $6 billion U.S. trade surplus," he said.
